deep.reconstruction:
The page holds three separate notes.

(1) Real singularities of algebraic space curves. This continues the last line of the previous page: 'Bei der algebraischen Raumcurve giebt es 8 Typen von reellen Singularitäten'.
- Setup: at a point P of a real analytic or algebraic branch, use the moving trihedron as coordinate frame. The x-axis is the tangent, the y-axis the principal normal, the z-axis the binormal.
- Normal form (my modern restatement): after a linear coordinate change the branch can be written as x = t^a + ..., y = t^b + ..., z = t^c + ..., with 1 <= a < b < c.
- a is the order of the point. b is the contact order with the tangent line. c is the contact order with the osculating plane z = 0.
- Hilbert's sentence 'the curve runs on in the direction of its tangent or turns back' is the parity of a.
- The three coordinate planes split space into 8 octants:
  - normal plane x = 0;
  - osculating plane z = 0;
  - rectifying plane y = 0. Hilbert names only the first two; this third plane is needed and is my addition.
- For t > 0 the branch lies in octant (+,+,+). For t < 0 it lies in octant ((-1)^a, (-1)^b, (-1)^c).
- So the 8 possible octants the curve can enter from correspond to the 8 parity patterns of (a, b, c). Equivalently, they correspond to the parities of the 'Wiener indices' (alpha0, alpha1, alpha2) = (a, b-a, c-b). Each index says whether the point, the tangent and the osculating plane respectively advance or turn back.
- Hilbert asks for 'the 8 shapes of the equations x, y, z = power series in t'. Smallest representatives, as (alpha0, alpha1, alpha2) -> (a, b, c):
  - (1,1,1) -> (1,2,3): ordinary point.
  - (1,1,2) -> (1,2,4): stationary osculating plane.
  - (1,2,1) -> (1,3,4): stationary tangent (inflection).
  - (2,1,1) -> (2,3,4): cusp (stationary point).
  - (1,2,2) -> (1,3,5).
  - (2,1,2) -> (2,3,5).
  - (2,2,1) -> (2,4,5).
  - (2,2,2) -> (2,4,6), realised with higher terms. Example: x = t^2, y = t^4 + t^5, z = t^6 + t^7. The leading exponents are then all even, and both half-branches enter the same octant.
- Second question, duality: 'how do these 8 types correspond dualistically?'
  - Dualising (point <-> osculating plane, tangent <-> tangent) sends (a, b, c) to (c-b, c-a, c). That is, it reverses (alpha0, alpha1, alpha2).
  - Hence the types with alpha0 ≡ alpha2 (mod 2) are self-dual: four of them.
  - The rest are exchanged in pairs. The cusp (2,1,1) is dual to the stationary osculating plane (1,1,2), and (2,1,2)-type... more precisely (2,2,1) <-> (1,2,2).
  - Example check (mine): for r = (t^2, t^3, t^4) the osculating-plane coordinates are proportional to (2t^2, -8/3 t, 1, -t^4/3). Their orders are 0, 1, 2, 4, so the dual exponents are (1, 2, 4), as the rule predicts.

(2) Hilbert's 'symbol [ ]' from his doctoral dissertation (Königsberg 1885, on invariant properties of special binary forms, especially spherical harmonics).
- He asks how this symbol is expressed through the composite operators DΔ or ΔD.
- Here D and Δ are the binary polarisation operators. In the standard (Aronhold/Cayley) usage, which I assume Hilbert follows, D = x1 ∂/∂x2 and Δ = x2 ∂/∂x1, acting on binary forms. Their commutator is DΔ - ΔD = x1∂1 - x2∂2, the weight operator.
- Hilbert expects such an expression to be not simpler but more convenient, and generalisable to ternary and higher substitutions. In modern terms: replace a dissertation-specific operator by an element of the universal enveloping algebra of sl2, which generalises to sl3 and beyond.
- The page gives no formula, so the precise identity cannot be reconstructed from this page.

(3) Research methodology.
- Of 100 equally good ideas perhaps one succeeds, and one cannot know in advance which.
- One must think a problem through until one can say exactly why one cannot proceed: which preliminary work, complicated for now but feasible, would be needed.
- At least one must solve the 'next higher question' 𝔅 = F^2. This refers back to the previous page's chain of questions A, B, C, ..., where B = 'can A be decided by finitely many operations?'.
- The page ends mid-sentence ('Die Mathematik hat anderen Wissenschaften gegen-'). It continues on the next page with the claim that in mathematics one can decide definitively whether a question is settled.
errors: Two planes (normal and osculating) give only 4 regions, not 8 octants. The rectifying plane (or the three trihedron planes together) is implicitly needed. This is a slip of formulation, not of substance.
Hilbert gives neither the 8 normal forms nor the duality on this page; both are posed only as questions, so there is nothing further to check.

If one insists on pure monomials x = t^a, y = t^b, z = t^c with gcd 1, only 7 parity types occur. The all-even type needs higher-order terms. Hilbert's wording 'power series of t' correctly allows for this.

results.what: Eight real local types of space-curve branches, distinguished by whether point, tangent and osculating plane advance or turn back (parities of the exponents a, b, c), equivalently by the octant of the moving trihedron the curve enters
results.modern_name: Local classification of real space-curve branches by characteristic (Wiener) indices / parity types; projective differential geometry of space curves
results.usually_credited_to: Christian Wiener (around 1880, with physical models), building on Möbius and von Staudt; popularised by F. Klein (Elementarmathematik vom höheren Standpunkte II)

results.what: Duality of the 8 types: (a, b, c) -> (c-b, c-a, c), i.e. reversal of (alpha0, alpha1, alpha2)
results.modern_name: Projective duality of space curves (dual curve via osculating planes)

results.what: Plan to express the dissertation operator [ ] through compositions DΔ or ΔD of the polarisation operators, for generalisation to ternary substitutions
results.modern_name: Expressing invariant-theoretic differential operators in the universal enveloping algebra of sl2 (Casimir-type expressions)
results.usually_credited_to: Aronhold, Cayley (Omega and polarisation operators); Hilbert's own 1885-1890 invariant-theory papers use D and Δ

results.what: Methodological maxim: analyse exactly why one cannot proceed and solve the next meta-question in the chain A, B, C, ... (decidability in finitely many steps)
results.modern_name: Early form of Hilbert's 'no ignorabimus' / meta-question programme (cf. Paris 1900 remarks on impossibility proofs)

deep.surprise_reason: The 8-type classification of space-curve singularities and its duality were classical by the 1880s (Wiener, Klein); Hilbert only poses them as exercises. The operator note is a private research plan without content. The methodological passage is a nice early private formulation of attitudes Hilbert later voiced publicly, but it is consistent with what is known of him.

checkable.asserts: The 8 representatives give 8 distinct sign patterns, i.e. the t<0 half-branch enters 8 different octants.
The osculating plane of the cusp (2,3,4) is (2t^2, -8t/3, 1, -t^4/3), so the dual exponents are (1,2,4) = (c-b, c-a, c).
The inflection type (1,3,4) has plane-coordinate orders giving dual exponents (1,3,4), i.e. it is self-dual (alpha = (1,2,1)).
